  - It allocates dest->unknown_chunks_data[i] with malloc of the same size.

- Buffer Overflow: The code allocates exactly src->unknown_chunks_size[i] bytes and then copies exactly that many bytes, so there is no out‐of‐bounds write in the copy loop.

original_information.commit_message:
proc: prevent accessing /proc/<PID>/environ until it's ready

If /proc/<PID>/environ gets read before the envp[] array is fully set up
in create_{aout,elf,elf_fdpic,flat}_tables(), we might end up trying to
read more bytes than are actually written, as env_start will already be
set but env_end will still be zero, making the range calculation
underflow, allowing to read beyond the end of what has been written.

Fix this as it is done for /proc/<PID>/cmdline by testing env_end for
zero.  It is, apparently, intentionally set last in create_*_tables().

This bug was found by the PaX size_overflow plugin that detected the
arithmetic underflow of 'this_len = env_end - (env_start + src)' when
env_end is still zero.

The expected consequence is that userland trying to access
/proc/<PID>/environ of a not yet fully set up process may get
inconsistent data as we're in the middle of copying in the environment
variables.

Separate repaint and layout requirements of StyleDifference (Step 1)

Previously StyleDifference was an enum that proximately bigger values
imply smaller values (e.g. StyleDifferenceLayout implies
StyleDifferenceRepaint). This causes unnecessary repaints in some cases
on layout change.

Convert StyleDifference to a structure containing relatively independent
flags.

This change doesn't directly improve the result, but can make further
repaint optimizations possible.

Step 1 doesn't change any functionality. RenderStyle still generate the
legacy StyleDifference enum when comparing styles and convert the result
to the new StyleDifference. Implicit requirements are not handled during
the conversion.

Converted call sites to use the new StyleDifference according to the
following conversion rules:
- diff == StyleDifferenceEqual (&& !context) => diff.hasNoChange()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaintObjectOnly()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint || diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaint() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff > StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsLayout()
- diff == StyleDifferencePositionedMovementLayoutOnly => diff.needsPositionedMovementLayoutOnly()
- diff == StyleDifferenceLayout => diff.needsFullLayout()

original_information.commit_message:
nEPT: Nested INVEPT

If we let L1 use EPT, we should probably also support the INVEPT instruction.

In our current nested EPT implementation, when L1 changes its EPT table
for L2 (i.e., EPT12), L0 modifies the shadow EPT table (EPT02), and in
the course of this modification already calls INVEPT. But if last level
of shadow page is unsync not all L1's changes to EPT12 are intercepted,
which means roots need to be synced when L1 calls INVEPT. Global INVEPT
should not be different since roots are synced by kvm_mmu_load() each
time EPTP02 changes.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function iterates over a list of directory entries (`pfpath->list`) in a file‐search path.
- For each entry it extracts the directory string (`pstr`, length `plen`) and attempts to form a candidate full filename by appending the requested `fname` (length `flen`) into a caller‐supplied `buffer` of length `blen`.
- If the directory string begins with ‘%’, it treats it as a special device prefix:
  • Parses the prefix into a `gs_parsed_file_name_t` (`pname`)  
  • Verifies the buffer is large enough for prefix + filename  
  • Concatenates prefix+filename into `buffer` and calls the device’s `open_file` routine.  
  • On success, it fills `buffer` again with the prefix+filename for the caller, sets `*pclen`, wraps the underlying stream in a PostScript file object, and returns 0.  
  • On failure it continues to the next path entry.
- For ordinary directory entries it calls `gp_file_name_combine` to build `buffer` = dir + “/” + fname, checking for success and that the result fits.
- It then calls `iodev_os_open_file` on the combined path.  
  • If the open succeeds, it enforces a permissions check (unless `starting_arg_file` is true).  
  • On permission success it records `*pclen` and returns the PostScript file stream.  
  • On permission failure it closes the stream and returns an `invalidfileaccess` error.
- If no directory entry yields a successful open, the function returns 1.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer overflow:  
  • The %device% branch checks `blen < max(pname.len, plen) + flen` before copying.  
  • The non‐device branch uses `gp_file_name_combine`, which itself enforces the buffer limit.  
  => No unchecked writes into `buffer` under normal integer ranges.
- Integer overflow:  
  • The sum `max(pname.len, plen) + flen` could in theory wrap if the lengths were adversarially large. In practice `plen` and `flen` are bounded by path‐length limits, so this is not a realistic attack surface.
- Path‐traversal / “..” collapsing:  
  • The routine delegates to `gp_file_name_combine` (which normally normalizes “../”) and to the special device parser as appropriate.  
  => No obvious unchecked “..” attack.
- Permission bypass / TOCTOU:  
  • The code opens the file first, then (unless it’s a starting_arg_file) checks permissions on the pathname. An attacker who races on the filesystem between open and check could substitute a different file.  
  => A classic TOCTOU race exists if an untrusted process can manipulate filesystem entries concurrently.
- Device‐prefix handling:  
  • The special‐device branch bypasses the OS‐level permission check entirely, trusting the device’s open routine to enforce any policy.
- Summary: There is no direct buffer overflow or unbounded write. The main residual risk is a race‐condition (open‑then‑check) and reliance on device code for security.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain a direct buffer‐overflow or path‐traversal vulnerability, though it does have a standard TOCTOU race between open and permission check.

original_information.commit_message:
ext4: use ext4_get_block_write in buffer write

Allocate uninitialized extent before ext4 buffer write and
convert the extent to initialized after io completes.
The purpose is to make sure an extent can only be marked
initialized after it has been written with new data so
we can safely drop the i_mutex lock in ext4 DIO read without
exposing stale data. This helps to improve multi-thread DIO
read performance on high-speed disks.

Skip the nobh and data=journal mount cases to make things simple for now.

Signed-off-by: Jiaying Zhang <jiayingz@google.com>
Signed-off-by: "Theodore Ts'o" <tytso@mit.edu>

attempting to reuse a previous ticket then a race condition can occur
potentially leading to a double free of the ticket data.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function Parse_lart takes a file position (pos) and a chunk size, seeks the file handle to that offset, and prepares to scan a DLS “LART” (list of articulation) chunk.  
   - It initializes two offsets (art1Pos, art2Pos) to zero.  
   - It computes endChunk = pos + size and then enters a loop while(pos < endChunk):  
     • It saves the current offset in chunkPos.  
     • It calls NextChunk(&pos, &temp, &size), which identifies the next sub-chunk ID in temp, returns that sub-chunk’s payload size in size, and advances pos past that chunk’s header.  
     • It switches on the chunk ID (temp):  
       – CHUNK_CDL: calls Parse_cdl to evaluate a conditional-list chunk; if Parse_cdl returns false (0), it aborts parsing and returns success (skips the rest of LART).  
       – CHUNK_ART1: records art1Pos = chunkPos + 8 (the data offset of the ART1 payload).  
       – CHUNK_ART2: similarly records art2Pos = chunkPos + 8.  
       – other IDs: ignored.  
   - After the loop, if art1Pos was set, it calls Parse_art at that offset; likewise for art2Pos.  
   - On any error return from the helper calls, it returns that error; otherwise it returns EAS_SUCCESS.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Integer-overflow on endChunk: endChunk = pos + size is computed in 32-bit signed arithmetic without overflow checks. A malicious size or pos near INT_MAX could wrap around, causing pos<endChunk logic to fail and potentially skip the scan or loop indefinitely.  
   - Zero-length or non-advancing chunks: if NextChunk ever returns size=0 and does not advance pos, the while(pos<endChunk) loop could spin infinitely. The code does not explicitly guard against that.  
   - Out-of-bounds seeks: art1Pos and art2Pos are set to chunkPos+8 regardless of the declared chunk size. If a chunk size <8 or chunkPos+8 > endChunk, later Parse_art might seek past the intended region or past end of file. The function itself does not validate that the chunk size is ≥8 before setting those offsets.  
   - Delegated parsing: actual reads happen in Parse_cdl, NextChunk, and Parse_art. If those routines fail to enforce bounds or lengths they receive, this routine may end up invoking them with bad parameters.  

   However, in this snippet no direct buffer writes occur; all data access is routed through the helper functions (which presumably perform their own bounds and error checks). The presence of the endChunk guard does limit the total scan region.  

3. Decision  
   No, there is no immediate exploitable flaw solely in this snippet. The primary risks (integer overflow on endChunk, potential infinite loop on zero-length chunks, and unguarded art-offset computation) would have to be combined with weaknesses in NextChunk/Parse_art to become a real vulnerability.

original_information.commit_message:
Implement a bubble that appears at the top of the screen when a tab enters 
fullscreen mode via webkitRequestFullScreen(), telling the user how to exit 
fullscreen. 

This is implemented as an NSView rather than an NSWindow because the floating 
chrome that appears in presentation mode should overlap the bubble. 

Content-initiated fullscreen mode makes use of 'presentation mode' on the Mac: 
the mode in which the UI is hidden, accessible by moving the cursor to the top 
of the screen. On Snow Leopard, this mode is synonymous with fullscreen mode. 
On Lion, however, fullscreen mode does not imply presentation mode: in 
non-presentation fullscreen mode, the chrome is permanently shown. It is 
possible to switch between presentation mode and fullscreen mode using the 
presentation mode UI control. 

When a tab initiates fullscreen mode on Lion, we enter presentation mode if not 
in presentation mode already. When the user exits fullscreen mode using Chrome 
UI (i.e. keyboard shortcuts, menu items, buttons, switching tabs, etc.) we 
return the user to the mode they were in before the tab entered fullscreen. 

BUG=14471

+// The FullscreenExitBubbleController manages the bubble that tells the user
+// how to escape fullscreen mode. The bubble only appears when a tab requests
+// fullscreen mode via webkitRequestFullScreen().
+@interface FullscreenExitBubbleController :
+    NSViewController<NSTextViewDelegate> {
+ @private
+  BrowserWindowController* owner_;  // weak
+  Browser* browser_; // weak
+
+ @protected
+  IBOutlet NSTextField* exitLabelPlaceholder_;
+
+  // Text fields don't work as well with embedded links as text views, but
+  // text views cannot conveniently be created in IB. The xib file contains
+  // a text field |exitLabelPlaceholder_| that's replaced by this text view
+  // |exitLabel_| in -awakeFromNib.
+  scoped_nsobject<NSTextView> exitLabel_;
+
+  scoped_nsobject<NSTimer> hideTimer_;
+  scoped_nsobject<NSAnimation> hideAnimation_;
+};

+#import <Cocoa/Cocoa.h>

+const int kPaddingPx = 8;
+const int kInitialDelayMs = 3800;
+const int kSlideOutDurationMs = 700;
+
+@interface FullscreenExitBubbleController (PrivateMethods)
+// Sets |exitLabel_| based on |exitLabelPlaceholder_|,
+// sets |exitLabelPlaceholder_| to nil.
+- (void)initializeLabel;
+
+- (void)hideSoon;
+
+// Returns the Accelerator for the Toggle Fullscreen menu item.
++ (ui::AcceleratorCocoa)acceleratorForToggleFullscreen;
+
+// Returns a string representation fit for display of
+// +acceleratorForToggleFullscreen.
++ (NSString*)keyCommandString;
+

+@implementation FullscreenExitBubbleController
+
+- (id)initWithOwner:(BrowserWindowController*)owner browser:(Browser*)browser {
+  if ((self = [super initWithNibName:@"FullscreenExitBubble"
+                              bundle:base::mac::MainAppBundle()])) {
+    browser_ = browser;
+    owner_ = owner;
+  }
+  return self;
+}
+
+- (void)awakeFromNib {
+  [self initializeLabel];
+  [self hideSoon];
+}
+
+- (void)positionInWindowAtTop:(CGFloat)maxY width:(CGFloat)maxWidth {
+  NSRect bubbleFrame = [[self view] frame];
+  bubbleFrame.origin.x = (int)(maxWidth/2 - NSWidth(bubbleFrame)/2);
+  bubbleFrame.origin.y = maxY - NSHeight(bubbleFrame);
+  [[self view] setFrame:bubbleFrame];
+}
+
+// Called when someone clicks on the embedded link.
+- (BOOL) textView:(NSTextView*)textView
+    clickedOnLink:(id)link
+          atIndex:(NSUInteger)charIndex {
+  browser_->ExecuteCommand(IDC_FULLSCREEN);
+  return YES;
+}
+
+- (void)hideTimerFired:(NSTimer*)timer {
+  NSRect endFrame = [[self view] frame];
+  endFrame.origin.y += endFrame.size.height;
+  endFrame.size.height = 0;
+  NSDictionary* dict = [NSDictionary dictionaryWithObjectsAndKeys:
+      [self view], NSViewAnimationTargetKey,
+      [NSValue valueWithRect:endFrame], NSViewAnimationEndFrameKey, nil];
+
+  NSViewAnimation* animation =
+      [[NSViewAnimation alloc]
+        initWithViewAnimations:[NSArray arrayWithObjects:dict, nil]];
+  [animation gtm_setDuration:kSlideOutDurationMs/1000.0
+                   eventMask:NSLeftMouseUpMask];
+  [animation setDelegate:self];
+  [animation startAnimation];
+  hideAnimation_.reset(animation);
+}
+
+- (void)animationDidEnd:(NSAnimation*)animation {
+  if (animation == hideAnimation_.get()) {
+    hideAnimation_.reset();
+  }
+}
+
+- (AnimatableView*)animatableView {
+  return static_cast<AnimatableView*>([self view]);
+}
+
+- (void)dealloc {
+  [hideAnimation_.get() stopAnimation];
+  [hideTimer_ invalidate];
+  [super dealloc];
+}
+
+@end

+@implementation FullscreenExitBubbleController (PrivateMethods)
+
+- (void)initializeLabel {
+  // Replace the label placeholder NSTextField with the real label NSTextView.
+  // The former doesn't show links in a nice way, but the latter can't be added
+  // in IB without a containing scroll view, so create the NSTextView
+  // programmatically.
+  exitLabel_.reset([[HyperlinkTextView alloc]
+      initWithFrame:[exitLabelPlaceholder_ frame]]);
+  [exitLabel_.get() setAutoresizingMask:
+      [exitLabelPlaceholder_ autoresizingMask]];
+  [[exitLabelPlaceholder_ superview]
+      replaceSubview:exitLabelPlaceholder_ with:exitLabel_.get()];
+  exitLabelPlaceholder_ = nil;  // Now released.
+  [exitLabel_.get() setDelegate:self];
+
+  NSString *message = l10n_util::GetNSStringF(IDS_EXIT_FULLSCREEN_MODE,
+      base::SysNSStringToUTF16([[self class] keyCommandString]));
+
+  [(HyperlinkTextView*)exitLabel_.get()
+        setMessageAndLink:@""
+                 withLink:message
+                 atOffset:0
+                     font:[NSFont systemFontOfSize:18]
+             messageColor:[NSColor whiteColor]
+                linkColor:[NSColor whiteColor]];
+
+  [exitLabel_.get() sizeToFit];
+  NSLayoutManager* layoutManager = [exitLabel_.get() layoutManager];
+  NSTextContainer* textContainer = [exitLabel_.get() textContainer];
+  [layoutManager ensureLayoutForTextContainer:textContainer];
+  NSRect textFrame = [layoutManager usedRectForTextContainer:textContainer];
+  NSRect frame = [[self view] frame];
+  NSSize textSize = textFrame.size;
+  frame.size.width = textSize.width + 2 * kPaddingPx;
+  [[self view] setFrame:frame];
+  textFrame.origin.x = textFrame.origin.y = kPaddingPx;
+  [exitLabel_.get() setFrame:textFrame];
+}
+
+// This looks at the Main Menu and determines what the user has set as the
+// key combination for quit. It then gets the modifiers and builds an object
+// to hold the data.
++ (ui::AcceleratorCocoa)acceleratorForToggleFullscreen {
+  NSMenu* mainMenu = [NSApp mainMenu];
+  // Get the application menu (i.e. Chromium).
+  for (NSMenuItem* menu in [mainMenu itemArray]) {
+    for (NSMenuItem* item in [[menu submenu] itemArray]) {
+      // Find the toggle presentation mode item.
+      if ([item tag] == IDC_PRESENTATION_MODE) {
+        return ui::AcceleratorCocoa([item keyEquivalent],
+                                    [item keyEquivalentModifierMask]);
+      }
+    }
+  }
+  // Default to Cmd+Shift+F.
+  return ui::AcceleratorCocoa(@"f", NSCommandKeyMask|NSShiftKeyMask);
+}
+
+// This looks at the Main Menu and determines what the user has set as the
+// key combination for quit. It then gets the modifiers and builds a string
+// to display them.
++ (NSString*)keyCommandString {
+  ui::AcceleratorCocoa accelerator =
+      [[self class] acceleratorForToggleFullscreen];
+  return [[self class] keyCombinationForAccelerator:accelerator];
+}
+
++ (NSString*)keyCombinationForAccelerator:(const ui::AcceleratorCocoa&)item {
+  NSMutableString* string = [NSMutableString string];
+  NSUInteger modifiers = item.modifiers();
+
+  if (modifiers & NSCommandKeyMask)
+    [string appendString:@"\u2318"];
+  if (modifiers & NSControlKeyMask)
+    [string appendString:@"\u2303"];
+  if (modifiers & NSAlternateKeyMask)
+    [string appendString:@"\u2325"];
+  BOOL isUpperCase = [[NSCharacterSet uppercaseLetterCharacterSet]
+      characterIsMember:[item.characters() characterAtIndex:0]];
+  if (modifiers & NSShiftKeyMask || isUpperCase)
+    [string appendString:@"\u21E7"];
+
+  [string appendString:[item.characters() uppercaseString]];
+  return string;
+}
+
+- (void)hideSoon {
+  hideTimer_.reset(
+      [[NSTimer scheduledTimerWithTimeInterval:kInitialDelayMs/1000.0
+                                        target:self
+                                      selector:@selector(hideTimerFired:)
+                                      userInfo:nil
+                                       repeats:NO] retain]);
+}

+  const CGFloat lineWidth = [self cr_lineWidth];
+
+  rect = NSOffsetRect([self bounds], 0, lineWidth*2);
+
+  NSPoint topLeft = NSMakePoint(NSMinX(rect), NSMaxY(rect));
+  NSPoint topRight = NSMakePoint(NSMaxX(rect), NSMaxY(rect));
+  NSPoint midLeft =
+      NSMakePoint(NSMinX(rect), NSMinY(rect) + kCurveSize);
+  NSPoint midRight =
+      NSMakePoint(NSMaxX(rect), NSMinY(rect) + kCurveSize);
+  NSPoint bottomLeft =
+      NSMakePoint(NSMinX(rect) + kCurveSize, NSMinY(rect));
+  NSPoint bottomRight =
+      NSMakePoint(NSMaxX(rect) - kCurveSize, NSMinY(rect));

+  [path moveToPoint:topLeft];
+  [path appendBezierPathWithArcWithCenter:NSMakePoint(bottomLeft.x, midLeft.y)
+      radius:kCurveSize startAngle:180 endAngle:270];
+
+  [path lineToPoint:bottomRight];
+  [path appendBezierPathWithArcWithCenter:NSMakePoint(bottomRight.x, midRight.y)
+      radius:kCurveSize startAngle:270 endAngle:360];
+  [path lineToPoint:topRight];
+
+  {
+    gfx::ScopedNSGraphicsContextSaveGState scopedGState;
+    [path addClip];
+
+    const NSRect bounds = [self bounds];
+
+    [[NSColor colorWithDeviceWhite:0 alpha:0.7] set];
+    NSRectFillUsingOperation(bounds, NSCompositeSourceOver);

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `wait_for_refresh(int offset, const char *prefix, int msec)` is designed to pause execution for a user‐specified delay while showing a live countdown in a console UI (when `as_console == TRUE`), or simply scheduling a timer callback (when `as_console == FALSE`).

- It computes `lpc = msec / 1000` to convert the millisecond delay into whole seconds and sets up a `timespec sleept = {1, 0}` for one‐second sleeps.

- If `as_console` is FALSE, it registers a GLib timeout handler (`mon_timer_popped`) to fire after `msec` milliseconds, stores the returned `timer_id`, and returns immediately (no console output).

- If `as_console` is TRUE, it logs a notice (`crm_notice`), then enters a loop that:
  • Uses ncurses calls (`move`, `printw`, `clrtoeol`, `refresh`) to display “<prefix>Refresh in Xs…” at the given screen line (`offset`),  
  • Decrements the second counter (`lpc--`),  
  • When `lpc` reaches zero, schedules one more 1 s GLib timeout and exits the loop; otherwise sleeps for one second via `nanosleep`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Format‐String Safety  
  The code always uses a constant format string (`"%sRefresh in %ds...\n"`) and supplies the user‐supplied `prefix` only as an argument to `%s`. There is no unfiltered user data in the format itself, so no classic format‐string vulnerability.

- Buffer Overflows / Bounds  
  `printw` writes directly into the curses window buffer; it will truncate or scroll lines according to the window’s width but does not overrun a fixed‐size local buffer. There is no stack‐allocated buffer being written, so no local overflow.

- Integer Handling  
  The division `msec / 1000` to compute `lpc` cannot overflow in a practically meaningful way given typical `int` ranges. If `msec` is negative, `lpc` becomes zero or negative, and the loop simply does not run—no crash or underflow.

- Race Conditions / Use‐After‐Free  
  Timer registration (`g_timeout_add`) and global `timer_id` assignment happen before returns. There is no concurrency on `timer_id` in this snippet, and the callback pointer is static (`mon_timer_popped, NULL`). No evident UAF or data‐race here.

- Denial of Service / Infinite Loop  
  The loop decrements `lpc` to zero; it cannot spin infinitely unless `msec` is extremely large (but still a finite signed‐int). The per‐iteration `nanosleep` guarantees we yield the CPU.

3. Decision

No, the code as shown does not contain any exploitable vulnerabilities. It correctly uses safe format strings, does not overflow buffers, and handles its timing logic without undefined behavior.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function tasklet_action_common() processes a chain of “tasklet” callbacks stored in tl_head.  
   - It first disables local interrupts, steals the entire list from tl_head, resets tl_head to empty, then reenables interrupts.  
   - It walks the stolen list one tasklet at a time:  
     • It tries to grab the tasklet’s lock (tasklet_trylock).  
     • If the lock is acquired and the tasklet’s atomic count is zero, it clears the “scheduled” state bit (or BUGs if it wasn’t set), invokes the tasklet’s func(data), then releases the lock and moves on.  
     • Otherwise (lock failed or count nonzero), it requeues the tasklet onto tl_head under interrupt‐disable, raises the softirq to ensure it will be retried later, and reenables interrupts.  
   - This continues until the list is exhausted.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Memory Safety: There is no unbounded indexing or buffer manipulation; the code only manipulates linked‐list pointers that it owns.  
   - Concurrency/Race Conditions:  
     • list head/tail updates are protected by disabling local interrupts.  
     • tasklet_trylock and atomic_read prevent concurrent execution of the same tasklet instance on multiple CPUs.  
     • Requeueing under irq‐disabled ensures the tasklet won’t be lost.  
   - Use of BUG(): The only panic path is if the tasklet_state bit logic is inconsistent, which would indicate a bug in tasklet book‐keeping, not an exploitable input flaw.  
   - No user‐controlled pointers or lengths are dereferenced; all state is maintained internally.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code contains no apparent vulnerability. It correctly serializes and requeues tasklets without unsafe memory or concurrency races.

original_information.Summary: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 4.17.2. The filter parsing in kernel/trace/trace_events_filter.c could be called with no filter, which is an N=0 case when it expected at least one line to have been read, thus making the N-1 index invalid. - The function raw_getfrag is a callback used to assemble fragments (header + payload) for a raw IP send.
- It interprets the opaque pointer from as a struct raw_frag_vec, which contains:
  - hlen: the length of a prebuilt IP header
  - hdr.c: a pointer to the header bytes
  - msg: an sk_buff or other message vector for the payload
- If the requested offset falls within the stored header (offset < hlen):
  - Compute how many header bytes to copy (copy = min(hlen – offset, len)).
  - If the skb is already checksummed (CHECKSUM_PARTIAL), do a straight memcpy of those header bytes into to.
  - Otherwise, update skb->csum by doing a partial-copy with checksum (csum_partial_copy_nocheck + csum_block_add).
  - Advance offset, to, and decrease len by the number of bytes copied.
  - If len reaches zero, return 0 (no further payload to copy).
- If any payload remains (or if offset ≥ hlen from the start):
  - Subtract the header length from offset
  - Delegate the remainder of the copy (payload bytes) to ip_generic_getfrag, passing along the adjusted offset, len, odd, and skb.

- Bounds checking for the header copy:
  - The code checks offset < hlen before accessing hdr.c + offset.
  - The copy length is capped at both the remaining header bytes (hlen – offset) and the caller’s len.
  - There is no out-of-bounds read or write in the header-copy path.
- Integer overflow concerns:
  - offset and len are int, but hlen is the known header size (small, positive).
  - offset + copy cannot exceed hlen or wrap, and offset − hlen is only done after ensuring offset ≥ hlen.
- Pointer validity and lifetime:
  - raw_frag_vec and its hdr.c buffer are managed by the raw‐socket transmit path; they remain valid for the duration of this call sequence.
- Checksum path:
  - memcpy is used only for CHECKSUM_PARTIAL skb states.
  - The other path uses csum_partial_copy_nocheck, which is designed for kernel‐space checksum handling.

  - Once the header portion is exhausted, the code hands off to the standard fragmentation helper, which itself does its own bounds/length checks.

No, the code does not contain a vulnerability. It correctly bounds-checks fragment offsets, caps copy lengths, and safely handles both checksum and non-checksum paths.

original_information.commit_message:
perf/core: Fix concurrent sys_perf_event_open() vs. 'move_group' race

Di Shen reported a race between two concurrent sys_perf_event_open()
calls where both try and move the same pre-existing software group
into a hardware context.

The problem is exactly that described in commit:

  f63a8daa5812 ("perf: Fix event->ctx locking")

... where, while we wait for a ctx->mutex acquisition, the event->ctx
relation can have changed under us.

That very same commit failed to recognise sys_perf_event_context() as an
external access vector to the events and thereby didn't apply the
established locking rules correctly.

So while one sys_perf_event_open() call is stuck waiting on
mutex_lock_double(), the other (which owns said locks) moves the group
about. So by the time the former sys_perf_event_open() acquires the
locks, the context we've acquired is stale (and possibly dead).

Apply the established locking rules as per perf_event_ctx_lock_nested()
to the mutex_lock_double() for the 'move_group' case. This obviously means
we need to validate state after we acquire the locks.

original_information.commit_message:
Fix integer overflow in layer_resize in map_engine.c (#268)

* Fix integer overflow in layer_resize in map_engine.c

There's a buffer overflow bug in the function layer_resize. It allocates
a buffer `tilemap` with size `x_size * y_size * sizeof(struct map_tile)`.
But it didn't check for integer overflow, so if x_size and y_size are
very large, it's possible that the buffer size is smaller than needed,
causing a buffer overflow later.

PoC: `SetLayerSize(0, 0x7FFFFFFF, 0x7FFFFFFF);`

Make MediaStreamDispatcherHost per-request instead of per-frame.

Instead of having RenderFrameHost own a single MSDH to handle all
requests from a frame, MSDH objects will be owned by a strong binding.

A consequence of this is that an additional requester ID is added to
requests to MediaStreamManager, so that an MSDH is able to cancel only
requests generated by it.

In practice, MSDH will continue to be per frame in most cases since
each frame normally makes a single request for an MSDH object.

This fixes a lifetime issue caused by the IO thread executing tasks
after the RenderFrameHost dies.

   - Integer vulnerabilities: The only arithmetic is a bitwise OR on an unsigned int; no overflow concern here beyond the usual fixed-width wrap, which in this context is harmless for bit masking.

3. Decision

1. Functional Analysis

The function `path_out` is the “output” handler for the PostgreSQL “path” data type. It does three things in sequence:

  • Retrieves its first argument as a `PATH *` via the macro  
    `PATH *path = PG_GETARG_PATH_P(0);`  
    This gives access to the internal `PATH` struct, which holds:  
      – `closed` (a flag indicating whether the path is closed or open)  
      – `npts`   (the number of points)  
      – `p`      (an array of point coordinates)  

  • Calls `path_encode(...)`, passing:  
      – A tag (either `PATH_CLOSED` or `PATH_OPEN` depending on `path->closed`)  
      – The integer `path->npts`  
      – The point-array pointer `path->p`  

    `path_encode` builds and returns a null-terminated C string representing the path (for example, “[(x1,y1),(x2,y2),…]” and possibly closing the loop).

  • Returns that C string to the caller with `PG_RETURN_CSTRING(...)`, which wraps it up as the function’s text output.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

  • Buffer overflows:  
    This snippet itself does no manual buffer handling; it delegates all string construction and allocation to `path_encode`. A well-written `path_encode` will measure the needed size (based on `npts`) and allocate a sufficiently large buffer in the current memory context. No raw `sprintf` or fixed-size array is used here.

  • Integer bounds or negative counts:  
    The code does not re-check `path->npts` or validate `path->p`, but those fields come from PostgreSQL’s own internally-constructed `PATH` datum. An invalid `PATH` struct should be impossible at this stage unless there is prior memory corruption elsewhere. Typical PG input routines enforce that `npts >= 0` and that the array pointer is valid.

  • Null‐pointer dereference:  
    `PG_GETARG_PATH_P(0)` guarantees a nonnull `PATH *` (or errors out earlier if the argument is NULL or wrong type). So `path` and its `p` array are assumed valid.

  • Injection or format‐string attacks:  
    No user‐supplied format strings are used. Numeric coordinates are serialized as text by `path_encode` under programmer control, so there is no uncontrolled format specifier vulnerability.

3. Decision

No, the snippet itself does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It simply retrieves an internal struct, hands its well‐defined fields to a helper routine for safe string‐building, and returns the result.

When opening files for write, ensure they aren't symbolic links

Issue #1048 identified that if, for example, a non privileged user
created a symbolic link from /etc/keepalvied.data to /etc/passwd,
writing to /etc/keepalived.data (which could be invoked via DBus)
would cause /etc/passwd to be overwritten.

This commit stops keepalived writing to pathnames where the ultimate
component is a symbolic link, by setting O_NOFOLLOW whenever opening
a file for writing.

This might break some setups, where, for example, /etc/keepalived.data
was a symbolic link to /home/fred/keepalived.data. If this was the case,
instead create a symbolic link from /home/fred/keepalived.data to
/tmp/keepalived.data, so that the file is still accessible via
/home/fred/keepalived.data.

There doesn't appear to be a way around this backward incompatibility,
since even checking if the pathname is a symbolic link prior to opening
for writing would create a race condition.

original_information.commit_message:
comics: Remove support for tar and tar-like commands

When handling tar files, or using a command with tar-compatible syntax,
to open comic-book archives, both the archive name (the name of the
comics file) and the filename (the name of a page within the archive)
are quoted to not be interpreted by the shell.

But the filename is completely with the attacker's control and can start
with "--" which leads to tar interpreting it as a command line flag.

This can be exploited by creating a CBT file (a tar archive with the
.cbt suffix) with an embedded file named something like this:
"--checkpoint-action=exec=bash -c 'touch ~/hacked;'.jpg"

CBT files are infinitely rare (CBZ is usually used for DRM-free
commercial releases, CBR for those from more dubious provenance), so
removing support is the easiest way to avoid the bug triggering. All
this code was rewritten in the development release for GNOME 3.26 to not
shell out to any command, closing off this particular attack vector.

This also removes the ability to use libarchive's bsdtar-compatible
binary for CBZ (ZIP), CB7 (7zip), and CBR (RAR) formats. The first two
are already supported by unzip and 7zip respectively. libarchive's RAR
support is limited, so unrar is a requirement anyway.

Discovered by Felix Wilhelm from the Google Security Team.

original_information.Summary: The (1) IPv4 and (2) IPv6 implementations in the Linux kernel before 3.1 use a modified MD4 algorithm to generate sequence numbers and Fragment Identification values, which makes it easier for remote attackers to cause a denial of service (disrupted networking) or hijack network sessions by predicting these values and sending crafted packets.
original_information.commit_message:
net: Compute protocol sequence numbers and fragment IDs using MD5.

Computers have become a lot faster since we compromised on the
partial MD4 hash which we use currently for performance reasons.

MD5 is a much safer choice, and is inline with both RFC1948 and
other ISS generators (OpenBSD, Solaris, etc.)

Furthermore, only having 24-bits of the sequence number be truly
unpredictable is a very serious limitation.  So the periodic
regeneration and 8-bit counter have been removed.  We compute and
use a full 32-bit sequence number.

For ipv6, DCCP was found to use a 32-bit truncated initial sequence
number (it needs 43-bits) and that is fixed here as well.

Reported-by: Dan Kaminsky <dan@doxpara.com>
Tested-by: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

original_information.Summary: The vmci_transport_dgram_dequeue function in net/vmw_vsock/vmci_transport.c in the Linux kernel before 3.9-rc7 does not properly initialize a certain length variable, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel stack memory via a crafted recvmsg or recvfrom system call.
original_information.commit_message:
VSOCK: vmci - fix possible info leak in vmci_transport_dgram_dequeue()

In case we received no data on the call to skb_recv_datagram(), i.e.
skb->data is NULL, vmci_transport_dgram_dequeue() will return with 0
without updating msg_namelen leading to net/socket.c leaking the local,
uninitialized sockaddr_storage variable to userland -- 128 bytes of
kernel stack memory.

Fix this by moving the already existing msg_namelen assignment a few
lines above.

+	$(AWK) 'BEGIN { files["."] = ""; dirs["."] = 1; } \
+	  { d=$$3; if (dirs[d] != 1) { print "d", d; dirs[d] = 1 } \

+# This directory's subdirectories are mostly independent; you can cd

+$(am__recursive_targets):
+	@fail=; \
+	if $(am__make_keepgoing); then \
+	  failcom='fail=yes'; \
+	else \
+	  failcom='exit 1'; \
+	fi; \
+	dot_seen=no; \
+	target=`echo $@ | sed s/-recursive//`; \
+	case "$@" in \
+	  distclean-* | maintainer-clean-*) list='$(DIST_SUBDIRS)' ;; \
+	  *) list='$(SUBDIRS)' ;; \
+	esac; \
+	for subdir in $$list; do \
+	  echo "Making $$target in $$subdir"; \
+	  if test "$$subdir" = "."; then \
+	    dot_seen=yes; \
+	    local_target="$$target-am"; \
+	  else \
+	    local_target="$$target"; \
+	  fi; \
+	  ($(am__cd) $$subdir && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) $$local_target) \
+	  || eval $$failcom; \
+	done; \
+	if test "$$dot_seen" = "no"; then \
+	  $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) "$$target-am" || exit 1; \
+	fi; test -z "$$fail"

+
+        NOTES relative to the implementation
+	====================================
+
+xsl:stylesheet:
+
+  all children except xsl:import can be in any order, so this
+can be stored as one big structure.
+
+xsl:include:
+  
+  this is really similar to XInclude, can be implemented as a
+nearly separate processing just after the XML stylesheet has been
+parsed.
+  Detect loops using a limited stack ...
+
+xsl:import:
+
+  seems this should be really implemented as having a stylesheet
+sublist being itself an import list
+
+  add the list at the end
+  when doing a resolution explore child before siblings in the list
+
+3 Data Model, we should operate on parsed trees
+
+3.1 No problem
+
+3.2 use the XML Base call, XSLT-1.1 references it
+
+3.4 Whitespace Stripping
+
+  Seems one may have to do a bit of preprocessing on both the
+stylesheet trees and the source trees.
+
+4 Expressions
+
+  looks okay, wondering about variable bindings though...
+  default namespace not in scope
+
+5.1 Processing Model
+
+  look in Michael Kay's book about how to efficiently find the
+template applying to a node. Might influence the in-memory stylesheet
+representation
+
+5.2 Patterns
+
+  the end of that section suggest that the expression could be computed in
+a simpler way. Maybe templates needs to be evaluated differently than
+through the normal XPath processing. This can be implemented separately
+or build an expression tree in the XPath module and use a different 
+evaluation mechanism. Not sure this is best.
+
+5.4 Applying Template Rules
+
+  xsl:apply-templates is the recurstion mechanism, note the select
+mechanism.
+
+  detection of loop: once the applied nodeset has been computed,
+check that none of the elements is part of the existing set in use, this
+may be costly and should be triggered only at a certain depth.
+
+5.5 Conflict Resolution for Template Rules
+
+  Sounds again that evaluation of a pattern rule should provide one
+more information not provided by the standard XPath evaluation
+
+5.6 Overriding Template Rules
+
+  another recursion mechanism, confirm that it is needed to separate
+the imported stylesheets.
+
+5.7 Modes
+
+  Confusing ??? need an example.
+
+6 Named Templates
+
+  No big deal it seems
+
+7.1.1 Literal Result Elements
+
+  cleanup of the namespace template should be done initially at stylesheet
+parsing.
+
+7.1.2 Creating Elements with xsl:element
+
+   okay, I bet it's usually used with { } expression computations
+
+7.1.3 Creating Attributes with xsl:attribute
+
+   need some running code to better understand all the subtilties
+
+7.1.4 Named Attribute Sets
+
+   Okay just a way to mimick param entities use fo attrib groups in Dtd's
+
+7.2 Creating Text
+
+   adjacent text nodes are merged ... okay
+   output escapeing might need a libxml API extension
+
+7.3 Creating Processing Instructions
+7.4 Creating Comments
+
+   RAS, one just need to make a couple of trivial checks
+
+7.5 Copying
+
+   Okay will need some testing
+
+7.6.1 Generating Text with xsl:value-of
+
+   will be a good test for XPath string() function
+   note in the example that the text nodes are coalesced
+
+7.6.2 Attribute Value Templates
+
+   hum, this is 
+    - contextual
+    - uses XPath
+
+  best seems to parse, generate an evaluation tree then evaluate
+when accessed. Note that multipe expressions can be associated to 
+a single attribute. Sounds like i will have to introduce a new
+element type inserted in the attribute nodelist. dohh ...
+
+7.7 Numbering
+
+  sounds interesting for users but might be costly, we will see ...
+
+7.7.1 Number to String Conversion Attributes
+
+   format="..." :-( it's gonna be painful ...
+
+8 Repetition
+9 Conditional Processing
+
+  doesn't sounds hard to implement since we are at an interpreter
+level but really useful in practice. Will be simple once the overall
+framework is set-up.
+
+10 Sorting
+
+  Okay applied to the node list of an xsl:apply-templates or xsl:for-each
+
+  The NOTEs are a bit scary ...
+
+11 Variables and Parameters
+
+   Variables can only be afttected at the top level, so it
+seems they act only as global variables ...
+   But this is by regions .... so some of the statements within
+a stylesheet my use a different set than others ... in practice
+it turns to be nearly like loacal variables ....
+  Need more thinking on this to handle it properly.
+  Might explain on of TOM's requests w.r.t. variable resolution
+
+11.1 Result Tree Fragments
+
+  Dohhh a new type ...
+  actually it's just a node set restricted type
+
+11.2 Values of Variables and Parameters
+
+  okay, real problem is scoping ...
+
+11.3 Using Values of Variables and Parameters with xsl:copy-of 
+
+  No surprize
+
+11.4 Top-level Variables and Parameters
+
+   It is an error if a stylesheet contains more than one binding
+   of a top-level variable with the same name and same import precedence
+
+   => ah ah, so it seems one can associate the variable bindings
+to a stylesheet and if needed recurse down the import list if not
+found, would simplify things a lot !
+
+   If the template or expression specifying the value of a global variable
+x references a global variable y, then the value for y must be computed
+before the value of x.
+
+   => Values can probably be computed dynamically at reference
+time, if this generate a loop, then it's an error. Lazy computations
+are great ...
+
+11.5 Variables and Parameters within Templates
+
+   
+   xsl:variable is allowed anywhere within a template that an instruction
+is allowed. In this case, the binding is visible for all following siblings
+and their descendants.
+   It is an error if a binding established by an xsl:variable or xsl:param
+element within a template shadows another binding established by an
+xsl:variable or xsl:param element also within the template.
+
+  => the example seems to imply that we can simply keep a list of
+     local variable binding to a template ... sounds fine.
+
+11.6 Passing Parameters to Templates
+
+  => Okay the parameter overrides the local binding
+
+12.1 Multiple Source Documents
+12.2 Keys
+
+  skipped for now
+
+12.3 Number Formatting
+
+  reimplementing Java formatting in C is gonna be a pain !
+
+12.4 Miscellaneous Additional Functions
+
+  current() => trivial
+
+  unparsed-entity-uri() => support in uri.c should do
+
+  generate-id() => use the in-memory address of the node ???
+
+  system-property() => sounds simple
+
+13 Messages
+
+  trivial I/Os
+
+14 Extensions
+15 Fallback
+
+   skipped for now
+
+16 Output
+
+16.1 XML Output Method
+
+  sounds that calling directly libxml output on the result tree
+should do it with a few caveats, for example one need to be
+able to parametrize the output
+
+16.2 HTML Output Method
+
+  sounds that calling libxml HTML output should do it too
+
+16.3 Text Output Method
+
+  doesn't sounds too hard ...
+
+16.4 Disabling Output Escaping
+
+  hum ... might be a bit painful to implement with the current framework."}<_**next**_>{"sha": "056d1961ee974f708960dfb3e8524b75c4a9c0f4", "filename": "third_party/libxslt/README.chromium", "status": "modified", "additions": 12, "deletions": 7, "changes": 19, "blob_url": "https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/96dbafe288dbe2f0cc45fa3c39daf6d0c37acbab/third_party/libxslt/README.chromium", "raw_url": "https://github.com/chromium/chromium/raw/96dbafe288dbe2f0cc45fa3c39daf6d0c37acbab/third_party/libxslt/README.chromium", "contents_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/chromium/chromium/contents/third_party/libxslt/README.chromium?ref=96dbafe288dbe2f0cc45fa3c39daf6d0c37acbab", "patch": "@@ -1,6 +1,6 @@

+install-man3: $(man_MANS)
+	@$(NORMAL_INSTALL)
+	@list1=''; \
+	list2='$(man_MANS)'; \
+	test -n "$(man3dir)" \
+	  && test -n "`echo $$list1$$list2`" \
+	  || exit 0; \
+	echo " $(MKDIR_P) '$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)'"; \
+	$(MKDIR_P) "$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)" || exit 1; \
+	{ for i in $$list1; do echo "$$i"; done;  \
+	if test -n "$$list2"; then \
+	  for i in $$list2; do echo "$$i"; done \
+	    | sed -n '/\.3[a-z]*$$/p'; \
+	fi; \
+	} | while read p; do \
+	  if test -f $$p; then d=; else d="$(srcdir)/"; fi; \
+	  echo "$$d$$p"; echo "$$p"; \
+	done | \
+	sed -e 'n;s,.*/,,;p;h;s,.*\.,,;s,^[^3][0-9a-z]*$$,3,;x' \
+	      -e 's,\.[0-9a-z]*$$,,;$(transform);G;s,\n,.,' | \
+	sed 'N;N;s,\n, ,g' | { \
+	list=; while read file base inst; do \
+	  if test "$$base" = "$$inst"; then list="$$list $$file"; else \
+	    echo " $(INSTALL_DATA) '$$file' '$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)/$$inst'"; \
+	    $(INSTALL_DATA) "$$file" "$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)/$$inst" || exit $$?; \
+	  fi; \
+	done; \
+	for i in $$list; do echo "$$i"; done | $(am__base_list) | \
+	while read files; do \
+	  test -z "$$files" || { \
+	    echo " $(INSTALL_DATA) $$files '$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)'"; \
+	    $(INSTALL_DATA) $$files "$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)" || exit $$?; }; \
+	done; }
+
+uninstall-man3:
+	@$(NORMAL_UNINSTALL)
+	@list=''; test -n "$(man3dir)" || exit 0; \
+	files=`{ for i in $$list; do echo "$$i"; done; \
+	l2='$(man_MANS)'; for i in $$l2; do echo "$$i"; done | \
+	  sed -n '/\.3[a-z]*$$/p'; \
+	} | sed -e 's,.*/,,;h;s,.*\.,,;s,^[^3][0-9a-z]*$$,3,;x' \
+	      -e 's,\.[0-9a-z]*$$,,;$(transform);G;s,\n,.,'`; \
+	dir='$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)'; $(am__uninstall_files_from_dir)

+ * Evaluate a precompiled XPath expression.
+ */
+static xmlXPathObjectPtr
+xsltPreCompEval(xsltTransformContextPtr ctxt, xmlNodePtr node,
+                xsltStylePreCompPtr comp) {
+    xmlXPathObjectPtr res;
+    xmlXPathContextPtr xpctxt;
+    xmlNodePtr oldXPContextNode;

+    oldXPProximityPosition = xpctxt->proximityPosition;
+    oldXPContextSize = xpctxt->contextSize;

+    oldXPNamespaces = xpctxt->namespaces;
+
+    xpctxt->node = node;
+#ifdef XSLT_REFACTORED
+    if (comp->inScopeNs != NULL) {
+        xpctxt->namespaces = comp->inScopeNs->list;
+        xpctxt->nsNr = comp->inScopeNs->xpathNumber;
+    } else {
+        xpctxt->namespaces = NULL;
+        xpctxt->nsNr = 0;
+    }
+#else
+    xpctxt->namespaces = comp->nsList;
+    xpctxt->nsNr = comp->nsNr;

+
+    res = xmlXPathCompiledEval(comp->comp, xpctxt);
+
+    xpctxt->node = oldXPContextNode;
+    xpctxt->proximityPosition = oldXPProximityPosition;
+    xpctxt->contextSize = oldXPContextSize;
+    xpctxt->nsNr = oldXPNsNr;
+    xpctxt->namespaces = oldXPNamespaces;
+
+    return(res);

+install-binSCRIPTS: $(bin_SCRIPTS)
+	@$(NORMAL_INSTALL)
+	@list='$(bin_SCRIPTS)'; test -n "$(bindir)" || list=; \
+	if test -n "$$list"; then \
+	  echo " $(MKDIR_P) '$(DESTDIR)$(bindir)'"; \
+	  $(MKDIR_P) "$(DESTDIR)$(bindir)" || exit 1; \
+	fi; \
+	for p in $$list; do \
+	  if test -f "$$p"; then d=; else d="$(srcdir)/"; fi; \
+	  if test -f "$$d$$p"; then echo "$$d$$p"; echo "$$p"; else :; fi; \
+	done | \
+	sed -e 'p;s,.*/,,;n' \
+	    -e 'h;s|.*|.|' \
+	    -e 'p;x;s,.*/,,;$(transform)' | sed 'N;N;N;s,\n, ,g' | \
+	$(AWK) 'BEGIN { files["."] = ""; dirs["."] = 1; } \
+	  { d=$$3; if (dirs[d] != 1) { print "d", d; dirs[d] = 1 } \
+	    if ($$2 == $$4) { files[d] = files[d] " " $$1; \
+	      if (++n[d] == $(am__install_max)) { \
+		print "f", d, files[d]; n[d] = 0; files[d] = "" } } \
+	    else { print "f", d "/" $$4, $$1 } } \
+	  END { for (d in files) print "f", d, files[d] }' | \
+	while read type dir files; do \
+	     if test "$$dir" = .; then dir=; else dir=/$$dir; fi; \
+	     test -z "$$files" || { \
+	       echo " $(INSTALL_SCRIPT) $$files '$(DESTDIR)$(bindir)$$dir'"; \
+	       $(INSTALL_SCRIPT) $$files "$(DESTDIR)$(bindir)$$dir" || exit $$?; \
+	     } \
+	; done

+# This directory's subdirectories are mostly independent; you can cd
+# into them and run 'make' without going through this Makefile.
+# To change the values of 'make' variables: instead of editing Makefiles,
+# (1) if the variable is set in 'config.status', edit 'config.status'

+$(am__recursive_targets):
+	@fail=; \
+	if $(am__make_keepgoing); then \
+	  failcom='fail=yes'; \
+	else \
+	  failcom='exit 1'; \
+	fi; \
+	dot_seen=no; \
+	target=`echo $@ | sed s/-recursive//`; \
+	case "$@" in \
+	  distclean-* | maintainer-clean-*) list='$(DIST_SUBDIRS)' ;; \
+	  *) list='$(SUBDIRS)' ;; \
+	esac; \
+	for subdir in $$list; do \
+	  echo "Making $$target in $$subdir"; \
+	  if test "$$subdir" = "."; then \
+	    dot_seen=yes; \
+	    local_target="$$target-am"; \
+	  else \
+	    local_target="$$target"; \
+	  fi; \
+	  ($(am__cd) $$subdir && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) $$local_target) \
+	  || eval $$failcom; \
+	done; \
+	if test "$$dot_seen" = "no"; then \
+	  $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) "$$target-am" || exit 1; \
+	fi; test -z "$$fail"

+	      -e "s|^$$topsrcdirstrip/|$(top_builddir)/|;t"`; \

+			   sed '/\//!d;s|^|$(distdir)/|;s,/[^/]*$$,,' | \

+	for file in $$dist_files; do \
+	  if test -f $$file || test -d $$file; then d=.; else d=$(srcdir); fi; \
+	  if test -d $$d/$$file; then \
+	    dir=`echo "/$$file" | sed -e 's,/[^/]*$$,,'`; \

+	    fi; \

+import io
+import os
+import sys
+import difflib
+
+from os import path
+from subprocess import Popen, PIPE
+
+xsltproc = path.join(os.getcwd(), "win32", "bin.msvc", "xsltproc.exe")
+if not path.isfile(xsltproc):
+    raise FileNotFoundError(xsltproc)
+
+def runtests(xsl_dir, xml_dir="."):
+    old_dir = os.getcwd()
+    os.chdir(xsl_dir)
+
+    for xsl_file in os.listdir():
+        if not xsl_file.endswith(".xsl"):
+            continue
+        xsl_path = "./" + xsl_file
+        name = path.splitext(xsl_file)[0]
+
+        xml_path = path.join(xml_dir + "/" + name + ".xml")
+        if not path.isfile(xml_path):
+            continue
+
+        args = [ xsltproc, xsl_path, xml_path ]
+        p = Popen(args, stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE)
+        out_path = path.join(xml_dir, name + ".out")
+        err_path = path.join(xml_dir, name + ".err")
+        out_diff = diff(p.stdout, "<stdout>", name + ".out")
+        err_diff = diff(p.stderr, "<stderr>", name + ".err")
+
+        if (len(out_diff) or len(err_diff)):
+            sys.stdout.writelines(out_diff)
+            sys.stdout.writelines(err_diff)
+            print()
+
+    os.chdir(old_dir)
+
+def diff(got_stream, got_name, expected_path):
+    text_stream = io.TextIOWrapper(got_stream, encoding="latin_1")
+    got_lines = text_stream.readlines()
+
+    if path.isfile(expected_path):
+        file = open(expected_path, "r", encoding="latin_1")
+        expected_lines = file.readlines()
+    else:
+        expected_lines = []
+
+    diff = difflib.unified_diff(expected_lines, got_lines,
+                                fromfile=expected_path,
+                                tofile=got_name)
+    return list(diff)
+
+print("## Running REC tests")
+runtests("tests/REC")
+
+print("## Running general tests")
+runtests("tests/general", "./../docs")
+
+print("## Running exslt common tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/common")
+
+print("## Running exslt functions tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/functions")
+
+print("## Running exslt math tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/math")
+
+print("## Running exslt sets tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/sets")
+
+print("## Running exslt strings tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/strings")
+
+print("## Running exslt dynamic tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/dynamic")
+
+print("## Running exslt date tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/date")
+"}<_**next**_>{"sha": "45c3e28f2f12f86861102f3b0f3f2367f5b1a3cc", "filename": "third_party/libxslt/xslt-config.in", "status": "removed", "additions": 0, "deletions": 137, "changes": 137, "blob_url": "https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/5d32c4d7ac9cd3e4a45a5cc1fc547103b66816c7/third_party/libxslt/xslt-config.in", "raw_url": "https://github.com/chromium/chromium/raw/5d32c4d7ac9cd3e4a45a5cc1fc547103b66816c7/third_party/libxslt/xslt-config.in", "contents_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/chromium/chromium/contents/third_party/libxslt/xslt-config.in?ref=5d32c4d7ac9cd3e4a45a5cc1fc547103b66816c7", "patch": "@@ -1,137 +0,0 @@

-void parsePath(const xmlChar *path) {

-	    return;
-	}
-	cur = path;
-	while ((*cur == ' ') || (*cur == ':'))
-	    cur++;
-	path = cur;
-	while ((*cur != 0) && (*cur != ' ') && (*cur != ':'))
-	    cur++;
-	if (cur != path) {
-	    paths[nbpaths] = xmlStrndup(path, cur - path);
-	    if (paths[nbpaths] != NULL)
-		nbpaths++;
-	    path = cur;
-	}
-    }

1. Functional Analysis

- The function begins by looking up the client’s pointer sprite (`PickPointer(client)->spriteInfo->sprite`).  
- It unpacks the protocol request (`REQUEST(xWarpPointerReq)`) to get source and destination window IDs, offsets, and clipping rectangles.  
- If a destination window ID is provided (`dstWid != None`), it calls `dixLookupWindow` to resolve and authorize that window.  
- It reads the sprite’s current “hot” (active) physical coordinates into `x` and `y`.  
- If a source window ID is provided:
  - It looks up and authorizes the source window.
  - It computes the window’s origin in global screen coordinates, adjusting if it is the root window of screen 0.
  - It checks whether the pointer’s current hot spot lies inside the specified source rectangle (srcX, srcY, srcWidth, srcHeight) and whether that point is “visible” via `XineramaPointInWindowIsVisible`.  If not, it bails out by returning `Success` (i.e., no warp).
- If a destination window is specified, it recomputes `x` and `y` to the window’s origin (again adjusting for screen 0’s root).
- It adds the client-supplied destination offsets (`dstX`, `dstY`) to the computed base coordinates.
- It clamps the resulting coordinates to the pointer’s allowed physical limits (`physLimits.x1..x2-1` and `y1..y2-1`).
- If the pointer sprite has a non-rectangular “hot shape,” it calls `ConfineToShape` to enforce that clipping.  
- Finally, it invokes `XineramaSetCursorPosition` to actually move the pointer, passing a flag (`TRUE`) to indicate that it’s a client-initiated warp.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Window lookups use `dixLookupWindow` with `DixReadAccess`, so arbitrary clients cannot warp the pointer relative to windows they do not have access to.  
- Bounds checking is applied:
  • The source filtering block ensures the pointer is already inside the specified source rectangle and, if not, simply skips the warp (no error path or crash).  
  • The computed destination is clamped to the sprite’s hard physical limits, preventing arithmetic from producing out-of-range coordinates.
- There are no unbounded memory accesses or string operations based on client data. All client-provided integers feed into simple arithmetic and bounds tests.  
- The function never dereferences a NULL window pointer: `dest` and `source` are only used when their lookups succeed.  
- Control flow always returns a well-defined status (`Success` or a lookup error code) and never leaks uninitialized data or leaves resources in an inconsistent state.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any obvious security vulnerabilities. It properly validates window IDs and permissions, bounds all client inputs, and confines pointer coordinates to safe limits.

1. Functional Analysis  
   a. The function `ClonePixelCacheRepository` takes two `CacheInfo` objects (`cache_info` and `clone_info`) plus an `ExceptionInfo`. It first checks for a “ping” cache and quick-returns. It then tests if the two caches share identical dimensions and channel state.  
   b. If both source and destination are in-memory (or memory‐mapped), it simply uses `memcpy()` to copy all pixels (and index data, if present) in one shot. If both are disk‐based caches, it calls `ClonePixelCacheOnDisk`.  
   c. If the caches differ in morphology (or type), it falls back to a row‐by‐row copy. It:  
      - Allocates per-thread “nexus” buffers for reading and writing.  
      - For each scanline (in parallel if OpenMP is enabled), reads a row of pixels from the source, zeroes out the destination row buffer, copies the data up to the minimum of the two widths, and writes it out.  
      - Repeats the same logic for the index channel if active.  
      - Cleans up the nexus buffers and logs a debug message if requested.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Integer overflow: The `length` for `memcpy` is computed as `min(source_columns, dest_columns) * sizeof(pixel)`. Because `min()` bounds it to the smaller of the two, and each row buffer is allocated to hold the full destination row, there is no out‐of‐bounds risk in normal operation.  
   - Buffer overflow: The code zeroes out the entire destination row buffer (`ResetMagickMemory` on a buffer sized to hold `clone_info->columns`) then only copies up to `length ≤ clone_info->columns * sizeof(pixel)`. That prevents overruns. The index‐channel copy uses the same logic.  
   - Resource exhaustion: The function aborts (`ThrowFatalException`) if it cannot allocate the nexus arrays, preventing silent heap corruption.  
   - Concurrency/race conditions: In the OpenMP path the shared `status` flag is tested and written without explicit atomic protection. In pathological cases this could lead to a data race on `status`, but the race only impacts early termination of the loop, not memory safety.  
   - Format‐string or injection: The only formatting is in a fixed debug log and uses safe locale formatting; no user‐controlled format specifier is introduced.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain any exploitable vulnerabilities under normal usage. The design bounds all `memcpy` lengths to buffer sizes, checks allocation results, and handles exceptional cases cleanly. exception.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function `gdImageCopyMerge` takes two images (`dst` and `src`), a source rectangle (specified by `srcX`, `srcY`, `w`, `h`), and a destination offset (`dstX`, `dstY`). It also takes a blending percentage `pct`.  
   - It iterates over each pixel `(x, y)` in the source rectangle.  
     - It fetches the source pixel color `c` via `gdImageGetPixel(src, x, y)`.  
     - If that color matches the source image’s transparent index, it skips blending for that pixel.  
     - Otherwise it reads the destination pixel color `dc` at `(tox, toy)`.  
     - It computes blended red, green, and blue channels by linearly interpolating between the source and destination channels, weighted by `pct` and `(100 – pct)`.  
     - It resolves (or allocates) the nearest matching palette index in the destination image for the newly computed RGB triplet via `gdImageColorResolve`.  
     - It writes that resulting color index to `(tox, toy)` using `gdImageSetPixel`.  
   - The loops advance `tox` across columns and then advance `toy` to the next row of the destination.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - *Out-of-bounds reads/writes*: The function does not explicitly clamp or validate that `(srcX + w) <= src->sx` or `(dstX + w) <= dst->sx`, nor for the vertical limits. If callers pass rectangles that extend beyond image boundaries, calls to `gdImageGetPixel` or `gdImageSetPixel` could index outside valid pixel storage. Proper GD-library internals may check bounds, but this snippet itself has no explicit range checks.  
   - *Integer overflow*: The calculations for `ncR`, `ncG`, and `ncB` use floating‐point multipliers `(pct / 100.0)`. There is no integer overflow risk in the arithmetic itself, but very large `pct` values (outside 0–100) would yield unexpected RGB values.  
   - *Resource exhaustion*: Each pixel’s blended color triggers a call to `gdImageColorResolve`, which may create new palette entries. In low-memory or limited-palette scenarios, repeatedly resolving thousands of nearly distinct colors could exhaust the palette or heap, potentially leading to failures or out-of-memory conditions.  
   - *Transparency safety*: The transparent‐color check correctly skips pixels matching `gdImageGetTransparent(src)`, so transparent‐pixel handling is properly done.  

   Overall, the snippet itself contains no direct memory corruption or injection vulnerability, but it relies on callers to supply valid rectangle dimensions. Without boundary checks here, out-of-bounds access is possible if upstream code fails to clip or validate coordinates.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code is not directly vulnerable in typical use, but it lacks explicit boundary checks on the source and destination rectangles, which could lead to out‐of‐bounds image accesses if invalid coordinates are supplied.

original_information.commit_message:
netfilter: ipv6: nf_defrag: drop mangled skb on ream error

Dmitry Vyukov reported GPF in network stack that Andrey traced down to
negative nh offset in nf_ct_frag6_queue().

Problem is that all network headers before fragment header are pulled.
Normal ipv6 reassembly will drop the skb when errors occur further down
the line.

netfilter doesn't do this, and instead passed the original fragment
along.  That was also fine back when netfilter ipv6 defrag worked with
cloned fragments, as the original, pristine fragment was passed on.

So we either have to undo the pull op, or discard such fragments.
Since they're malformed after all (e.g. overlapping fragment) it seems
preferrable to just drop them.

Same for temporary errors -- it doesn't make sense to accept (and
perhaps forward!) only some fragments of same datagram.

Fixes: 029f7f3b8701cc7ac ("netfilter: ipv6: nf_defrag: avoid/free clone operations")

1. Functional Analysis  
   The function gen_init_key() performs a mutual‐authentication and session‐key derivation sequence between a host and a secure‐card:

   • Preconditions and setup  
     – Validates that card->drv_data is non‐NULL and retrieves exdata (driver state)  
     – Prepares an APDU (case 4 short) with CLA=0x80, INS=0x50, and sends 8 bytes of host random (g_random)  
     – Temporarily forces the secure‐card transport mode to “plain” (no secure messaging)  
     – Transmits the APDU, then restores the prior transport mode  

   • Reception of card challenge  
     – Host receives 28 bytes of response into result[]  
       * result[12..19] is the card’s 8‐byte random challenge  
       * result[16..19] the first 4 bytes, and result[20..27] the card cryptogram  

   • Step 1: Build “derivation data”  
     – data[0..3]   = result[16..19]   (card random [4..7])  
     – data[4..7]   = g_random[0..3]   (host random [0..3])  
     – data[8..11]  = result[12..15]   (card random [0..3])  
     – data[12..15] = g_random[4..7]   (host random [4..7])  

   • Step 2 & 3: Derive S-ENC and S-MAC session keys  
     – If key_type==AES:  
         new SK_ENC = AES-ECB(encryption of data under exdata->sk_enc)  
         new SK_MAC = AES-ECB(encryption of data under exdata->sk_mac)  
       Else (3DES):  
         similarly with 3DES-ECB  

   • Step 4: Compute host cryptogram  
     – Builds data′ = host_random[0..7] ∥ card_random[0..7], then ISO 9797-1 padding: 0x80 | 0x00…  
     – Encrypts data′ under SK_ENC in CBC mode with IV=0  
     – The last block of the CBC output (cryptogram[16..]) is the host cryptogram  

   • Final check  
     – Compares the host cryptogram (offset 16, length =8) against the card cryptogram result[20..27]  
     – Returns SC_SUCCESS if they match, else SC_ERROR_CARD_CMD_FAILED  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   • Memory safety  
     – data[256] and cryptogram[256] are large enough for all writes (max 32 bytes used)  
     – result, key_enc, key_mac are assumed valid pointers; no out-of-bounds writes occur here  

   • Cryptographic correctness  
     – Uses a standard challenge–response pattern (host+card nonces)  
     – Derives two distinct session keys by encrypting the same “derivation data” under two different base keys (sk_enc vs sk_mac)  
     – Pads according to ISO 9797-1 Method 2 and uses zero IV for a pure cryptogram  
     – Verification is limited to an 8-byte fragment; protocols often do the same  

   • Potential minor issues  
     – The final memcmp of 8 bytes is not constant‐time, so in a high‐threat environment a side‐channel attacker observing timing might glean mismatch position. In most smart‐card contexts this is not a practical concern.  
     – Reliance on a global g_random buffer: the security depends entirely on how g_random was generated; if g_random is reused or predicted, replay or impersonation could follow. That, however, is outside this snippet.  
     – No explicit clearing of sensitive session keys or intermediate buffers after use, though on many embedded platforms zeroing on stack reuse is possible.  

   Overall, the code follows a standard ISO/IEC style key‐derivation and challenge–response. There are no obvious buffer overflows, improper pointer uses, or cryptographic mis-implementations in this snippet.

3. Decision  
   No, I do not identify any exploitable vulnerabilities in this code as written.

  - On entry it saves the current address-limit segment (old_fs), then picks which native ioctl command (kcmd) and which local struct pointer (karg) to use based on the 32-bit command it received.
  - It sets the address-limit to KERNEL_DS so that the upcoming sys_ioctl invocation will treat the karg pointer as a kernel-space pointer.
  - It calls sys_ioctl(fd, kcmd, karg).  If that returns an error, it restores the old address-limit and returns the error.
  - On success, it switches again on the original cmd to do the appropriate copy-out:
    • For MTIOCPOS32, it copies pos.mt_blkno into the user’s upos32->mt_blkno field  
    • For MTIOCGET32, it copies out each field of struct mtget (mt_type, mt_resid, …, mt_blkno) into the corresponding fields of the user’s mtget32 struct  
    All of the user copies use __put_user(), which will fault safely if the user address is invalid.
  - It returns 0 on success or -EFAULT if any __put_user fails.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

  - Address-limit changes: The code correctly saves old_fs, sets KERNEL_DS only for the sys_ioctl call, then restores old_fs. There is no window in which user data is mistakenly treated as kernel data.
  - sys_ioctl call: Passing a kernel‐space pointer under KERNEL_DS is exactly the intended use. The ioctl implementation will use that pointer safely.
  - Copy‐out to user: Uses __put_user(), which checks the user pointer and returns –EFAULT on faults. There is no unbounded loop or buffer that could overflow.
  - There is no use-after-free or race window involving the local stack buffers, because they remain valid until the copy‐out is complete.
  - No unchecked user-supplied integer is used to index or allocate memory, so there is no integer overflow or similar.
  - All code paths restore the address limit and return standard error codes on failure.

3. Decision

  No, this code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It correctly handles address-limit switching, calls sys_ioctl safely, and uses __put_user for secure copy‐out.

respond_before:
1. Functional Analysis

- The method `ConvertToCustomHistogramName` takes a C‐string `histogram_name` as input.
- It constructs a `std::string name` from that C‐string.
- It checks two conditions:
  a. That `common_host_histogram_suffix_` is not empty.  
  b. That `name` is present in the `custom_histograms_` collection.  
- If both conditions hold, it appends `common_host_histogram_suffix_` to `name`.
- It returns the (possibly modified) `name`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory safety / buffer overflow: Uses `std::string` for all string operations, so there is no raw buffer‐overflow risk.
- Injection / parsing: The code merely renames histograms; it does not execute or parse the string in a security‐sensitive context, so no injection vector is obvious.
- Denial of service / resource exhaustion: An attacker could supply an extremely long `histogram_name` or suffix, but this only consumes heap memory in a bounded way; it’s not exceptional compared to any other `std::string` usage.
- Null‐pointer dereference: If `histogram_name` is a null pointer, the `std::string` constructor has undefined behavior. In normal use, `histogram_name` should always be a valid C‐string.
- Thread safety: The snippet is `const`, but if `custom_histograms_` or `common_host_histogram_suffix_` are mutated concurrently elsewhere without synchronization, that would be a thread-safety issue (not specific to this code).

3. Decision

No, the code as shown does not contain any exploitable vulnerabilities. It safely manages memory via `std::string` and only appends a suffix under well‐defined conditions. The only caveat is that passing a null `histogram_name` would be undefined behavior.

1. Functional Analysis

- The method setMinimumSizeForResizing takes a LayoutSize object (size) as input.
- It checks two conditions in the if statement:
  a. hasRareData(): a predicate that returns true if the Element already has an allocated “rare data” structure.
  b. size == defaultMinimumSizeForResizing(): whether the requested minimum size matches the class’s default.
- If the Element has no rare data and the requested size equals the default, the method returns immediately (no work needed).
- Otherwise, it calls ensureElementRareData(), which lazily allocates or retrieves the rare-data structure, and then stores the new size via setMinimumSizeForResizing(size).

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory safety:  
  • There is no manual buffer manipulation or raw pointer arithmetic here.  
  • ensureElementRareData() presumably handles any allocation internally; if it fails it would throw or handle its own errors.  
- Input validation:  
  • The code does not validate LayoutSize beyond comparing it to a default value, but it also does not use it in a way that could overflow or underflow.  
- Concurrency:  
  • No locking or threading primitives are shown; if this class were used concurrently, it would need external synchronization, but that is beyond the snippet.  
- Injection or code‑execution risks:  
  • No user‑supplied code or format strings are executed.  
- Resource leaks:  
  • Raredata lifetime is managed internally; no obvious leaks.

Overall, the code is straightforward data storage logic without string or buffer operations, without use of untrusted input in a dangerous context, and without raw memory access.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain vulnerabilities. It safely checks for a default­-value short‑circuit, allocates on demand, and stores the provided size without unsafe operations.

respond_before:
1. Functional Analysis  
- The function blkg_prfill_stat takes three arguments:  
  • sf: a pointer to a seq_file (used for formatted output in the kernel’s seq_file interface)  
  • pd: a pointer to a blkg_policy_data structure  
  • off: an integer byte‐offset within that structure  
- It computes a pointer to the field at byte‐offset off by doing (void *)pd + off.  
- It calls blkg_stat_read() on that address to fetch a 64‐bit statistic.  
- Finally it passes sf, pd, and the retrieved value into __blkg_prfill_u64(), which formats/prints the 64‐bit value into the seq_file and returns the value.

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
- Pointer arithmetic: Casting pd to (void *) and adding an arbitrary int offset could, in principle, walk off either end of the structure if off is out of range.  
- In practice, blkg_prfill_stat is only ever called from within the kernel with compile‐time constants or well‐validated offsets (e.g. generated via offsetof on known fields).  
- There is no user‐supplied data driving pd or off; both are internal kernel values.  
- No unchecked input, no string operations, no memory allocation, no arithmetic wrap‐around on off in normal usage, and no direct user pointers involved.  
- Therefore, under normal kernel usage there is no exploitable memory corruption, out‐of‐bounds read, or other vulnerability here.

3. Decision  
No, the code does not contain a vulnerability—its use of pointer arithmetic is controlled by internal, validated offsets and there is no untrusted input.

respond_before:
1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function `png_write_init` takes a single argument, `png_ptr`, which is a pointer to a PNG write structure.  
   - It exists solely to support applications that were compiled against libpng versions earlier than 1.0.7.  
   - Inside, it calls the newer initialization routine `png_write_init_2`, passing:  
     • the same write-structure pointer (`png_ptr`)  
     • the string `"1.0.6 or earlier"` as the version identifier  
     • two zero parameters (presumably default flags for chunks or I/O settings)  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - No user‐supplied or external data is read or parsed in this stub; it simply forwards fixed values into `png_write_init_2`.  
   - There are no buffer operations, string concatenations, or integer arithmetic that could overflow or be manipulated.  
   - Control flow is straightforward with no branching on untrusted input, and no resources are allocated or freed improperly here.  

3. Decision  
   No, this code does not contain any vulnerabilities. It’s a simple backward‐compatibility wrapper that safely delegates to the newer initializer.

original_information.commit_message:
Btrfs: make xattr replace operations atomic

Replacing a xattr consists of doing a lookup for its existing value, delete
the current value from the respective leaf, release the search path and then
finally insert the new value. This leaves a time window where readers (getxattr,
listxattrs) won't see any value for the xattr. Xattrs are used to store ACLs,
so this has security implications.

This change also fixes 2 other existing issues which were:

*) Deleting the old xattr value without verifying first if the new xattr will
   fit in the existing leaf item (in case multiple xattrs are packed in the
   same item due to name hash collision);

*) Returning -EEXIST when the flag XATTR_CREATE is given and the xattr doesn't
   exist but we have have an existing item that packs muliple xattrs with
   the same name hash as the input xattr. In this case we should return ENOSPC.

A test case for xfstests follows soon.

Thanks to Alexandre Oliva for reporting the non-atomicity of the xattr replace
implementation.

Reported-by: Alexandre Oliva <oliva@gnu.org>
Signed-off-by: Filipe Manana <fdmanana@suse.com>

1. Functional Analysis

The function `mptsas_process_scsi_task_mgmt` handles incoming SCSI Task Management messages for an MPT SAS HBA in QEMU. Broadly, it does the following:

- Adjusts byte‐order on the request (`mptsas_fix_scsi_task_mgmt_endianness`).
- Assembles a zeroed‐out reply structure and copies over header fields (TargetID, Bus, Function, etc.).
- Dispatches based on the requested TaskType:

  a. ABORT_TASK / QUERY_TASK  
     - Locates the target SCSI device (bus, target ID, LUN).  
     - Validates the LUN.  
     - Searches the device’s pending request queue for one matching `TaskMsgContext`.  
     - If QUERY: immediately succeeds if the request is present.  
     - If ABORT: allocates an “async” reply, registers a notifier, calls `scsi_req_cancel_async`, then jumps to reply logic.

  b. ABRT_TASK_SET / CLEAR_TASK_SET  
     - Same device/LUN find & check.  
     - Allocates an async reply.  
     - Iterates all pending requests on that LUN, registers a notifier for each cancel, and tallies `count`.  
     - Falls through to shared “maybe‐async” reply code.

  c. LOGICAL_UNIT_RESET  
     - Finds the device, checks the LUN, then calls `qdev_reset_all` on that unit.

  d. TARGET_RESET  
     - Validates Bus == 0 and TargetID ≤ max_devices.  
     - Iterates all devices on channel 0 matching the TargetID and calls `qdev_reset_all`.

  e. RESET_BUS  
     - Calls `qbus_reset_all` to reset the entire bus.

  f. default  
     - Replies “not supported.”

- The “reply_maybe_async” block handles the case where there may be multiple in‐flight cancels. If not all have completed yet, it returns without posting a reply; otherwise it frees the async reply buffer, fills in `TerminationCount`, and continues.
- Finally (label `out:`) it byte‐swaps the reply back, then posts it via `mptsas_post_reply`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer and size safety  
  – Compile‐time asserts (`QEMU_BUILD_BUG_ON`) ensure the doorbell buffers are large enough and that `sizeof(*req)` / `sizeof(reply)` cannot overflow.  
  – All `memcpy`/`memset`/`g_memdup` uses the exact `sizeof` of the structs, so there is no overflow risk there.

- Bounds checks  
  – Bus and TargetID are checked before TARGET_RESET.  
  – LUN is verified against the device’s stored `sdev->lun`.  
  – The code never dereferences out‐of‐bounds pointers or jumps past array edges.

- Integer overflow / underflow  
  – Counts are kept in a plain `int`. Worst‐case queue lengths on a SCSI HBA are far below `INT_MAX`.  
  – No arithmetic on lengths or counts that could wrap.

- Memory management  
  – Async replies (`reply_async`) are either freed in the synchronous path (when no outstanding cancels) or by the cancel notifier callback once all cancellations complete.  
  – There is no code path that leaks or double‐frees the async reply.

- Concurrency / race conditions  
  – QEMU’s I/O thread model serializes HBA commands; the request queue is only walked and mutated under that thread’s control.  
  – Notifications and callback bookkeeping (`MPTSASCancelNotifier`) are standard QEMU patterns with no known reentrancy holes here.

In summary, the code performs all expected bounds checks, uses fixed‐size buffers, and manages its dynamic memory in a disciplined way. There is no indication of buffer overflows, integer wrapping, UAF, or other common C vulnerabilities.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any obvious security vulnerabilities. It correctly validates inputs, manages memory, and handles asynchronous cancellations safely.

  - The function stretch() rescales an in-memory image buffer according to a global pixel_aspect ratio.  
  - If pixel_aspect == 1, it does nothing. Otherwise it prints “Stretching the image…”.  
  - When pixel_aspect < 1, it computes a new height (newdim), allocates a new image array of size width × newdim, and for each output row runs a simple linear interpolation in the vertical direction between two source rows. It then updates height = newdim.  
  - When pixel_aspect > 1, it similarly computes a new width (newdim), allocates a new image array of size newdim × height, and for each output column interpolates horizontally between two source columns. It then updates width = newdim.  
  - In both cases it frees the old image buffer, assigns image = the newly allocated buffer, and returns.

  - Memory bounds: the loops that write into img run row in [0..newdim) and col in [0..width) (or vice-versa), matching the allocation size of width × newdim (or newdim × height), so there is no out-of-bounds access under normal conditions.

  - Integer overflow: newdim is stored in a ushort and width*newdim is passed to calloc. If width or newdim were large enough to overflow a 16-bit ushort or to overflow size_t arithmetic, one could under-allocate and then overrun the buffer. In practice width and height are usually well within safe bounds, and no unbounded user input goes into pixel_aspect, width, or height in this snippet.  
  - Pointer arithmetic: pix0 and pix1 are computed so as never to step outside the original image buffer (the code clamps the “next” row or column to the same pointer at the edges).
